summary:
Orbiscope is a satellite-based wildfire monitoring and analytical platform developed for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots.”

The project brings together active-fire detections from NASA's MODIS (Terra and Aqua) and VIIRS (Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21) instruments through NASA FIRMS. It provides an interactive map, customizable Area of Interest (AOI), historical data exploration, daily activity heatmaps, and monthly and yearly visualizations.

Orbiscope addresses differences between satellite sensors by introducing a sensor-balanced temporal activity index that helps users compare detection patterns across sensor groups. Additional analytical features include seasonal comparisons, statistical anomaly detection, and a relative observation-activity score combining detection counts and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).

The platform also includes CSV export, multilingual support, data caching, NASA FIRMS usage monitoring, and background processing for historical queries.

Orbiscope is designed to make satellite fire information more accessible and understandable for researchers, environmental organizations, students, and decision-makers. It supports exploratory analysis and situational awareness; its indicators are not official fire-danger ratings, fire forecasts, or emergency alerts. Active-fire detections should not be interpreted as burned-area measurements.
details:
Orbiscope – Project Details

1. Introduction

Orbiscope is an interactive satellite-based wildfire monitoring and analytical platform developed by the Orbiscope Development Team for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 challenge, “Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots.”

The project focuses on bringing together active-fire observations from multiple satellite instruments and making their temporal and spatial patterns easier to explore and interpret.

2. Problem Statement

Satellite instruments such as MODIS and VIIRS provide valuable active-fire observations. However, their detections differ in spatial resolution, observation timing, scan geometry, and detection characteristics.

These differences can make direct comparisons between satellite datasets difficult. Users may also struggle to explore historical fire activity, identify unusual patterns, and understand how observations vary across different periods and sensors.

Orbiscope addresses this challenge by providing a unified environment for exploring, comparing, and analyzing MODIS and VIIRS active-fire detections.

3. Data Sources

The platform retrieves active-fire data through NASA's Fire Information for Resource Management System (FIRMS), using its Area CSV API.

Supported satellite data sources include:

  • MODIS Terra
  • MODIS Aqua
  • VIIRS Suomi-NPP
  • VIIRS NOAA-20
  • VIIRS NOAA-21

The platform supports near-real-time and standard-processing datasets where available.

Important observation attributes include geographic coordinates, acquisition date and time, satellite source, confidence, brightness temperature, and Fire Radiative Power (FRP).

4. Main Features

Interactive Fire Map: Displays active-fire detections geographically using an interactive Leaflet map.

Custom Area of Interest: Users can define and edit a geographic bounding box to investigate a selected region.

Multi-Sensor Exploration: Users can explore detections from MODIS Terra/Aqua and VIIRS Suomi-NPP, NOAA-20, and NOAA-21.

Historical Analysis: Supports historical exploration over date ranges of up to ten years, subject to source-data availability.

Activity Heatmap: A calendar-style visualization presents daily fire-detection activity and helps users identify periods of increased activity.

Temporal Analytics: Monthly and yearly charts help reveal changes in active-fire observations over time.

Seasonal Comparison: Compares activity on similar days of the year across different years to identify potentially unusual seasonal patterns.

Statistical Anomaly Detection: Uses descriptive statistical analysis, including z-scores, to highlight unusually high observation counts.

Sensor-Balanced Temporal Activity Index: Normalizes daily detections within each sensor group, averages the sensor-group shares, and scales the resulting temporal pattern to a 0–100 range. This helps compare temporal activity patterns without treating raw sensor counts as directly equivalent measurements.

Relative Observation-Activity Score: Combines normalized detection counts and normalized FRP using a weighted approach (70% detections and 30% FRP) to provide an exploratory relative activity indicator.

CSV Export: Allows users to export retrieved fire-observation records for further analysis.

Multilingual Interface: Supports English, Azerbaijani, and Russian.

System Monitoring: Includes NASA FIRMS usage monitoring, cache statistics, and background job status information.

5. Harmonization Methodology

The project's central analytical approach is to reduce the impact of differences in the number of observations contributed by different sensor groups when comparing temporal patterns.

Instead of directly comparing raw detection counts, Orbiscope calculates each sensor group's share of its own detections over the selected period. These normalized daily shares are then averaged across sensor groups and scaled for visualization.

This method helps users explore whether fire-observation activity changes over time in a similar or different way across satellite groups.

It is important to clarify that this is an analytical normalization approach, not a physical or radiometric cross-calibration of MODIS and VIIRS instruments. Differences in spatial resolution, overpass timing, detection probability, cloud cover, scan geometry, and other sensor characteristics remain relevant.

6. Technical Architecture

Orbiscope is developed using:

  • Python and Flask for the backend and API services.
  • NASA FIRMS Area CSV API for satellite fire observations.
  • SQLite for local data caching.
  • HTML, CSS, and JavaScript for the user interface.
  • Leaflet for interactive geographic visualization.
  • Charting and data-processing logic for temporal and statistical analysis.

The backend provides endpoints for health checks, fire-data retrieval, background jobs, FIRMS usage information, and cache statistics.

Historical requests are processed using background jobs and bounded concurrency. The application includes retry and backoff handling for temporary API errors and monitors usage to reduce unnecessary requests.

The NASA FIRMS MAP_KEY is intended to remain server-side rather than being exposed in the browser.

7. Analytical Interpretation and Limitations

Orbiscope analyzes active-fire detections, which represent satellite-observed thermal anomalies. They are not equivalent to confirmed fire perimeters or burned-area measurements.

The seasonal comparison is an exploratory baseline rather than a validated climatological model. The z-score threshold is descriptive and does not independently establish a fire emergency.

The relative observation-activity score is not a fire-behavior forecast, official fire-danger rating, or public warning system. Its purpose is to support exploratory analysis and situational awareness.

8. Intended Users and Impact

The platform is intended for:

  • Environmental researchers and analysts.
  • Students and educators.
  • Environmental organizations.
  • People interested in satellite remote sensing.
  • Decision-makers who need accessible exploratory views of fire observations.

By making multi-sensor satellite observations easier to explore, Orbiscope aims to support environmental awareness, data literacy, and more informed investigation of wildfire activity.

9. Future Development

Potential future improvements include:

  • Additional satellite and environmental datasets.
  • More advanced sensor harmonization methods.
  • Integration of meteorological and land-cover information.
  • Improved spatial and temporal comparison tools.
  • More comprehensive validation against independent reference datasets.
  • Deployment as a publicly accessible platform.

10. Conclusion

Orbiscope transforms NASA FIRMS active-fire observations into an accessible multi-sensor exploration and analysis environment. Its main contribution is a practical workflow for examining MODIS and VIIRS observations together while making the limitations of cross-sensor comparison explicit.
